name: General trivia (easy)
description: 50 easy questions about a broad mix of everyday knowledge that fits none of the other categories. Written by Claude from cited web pages; every question names its page. Checked by a second model pass; the questions it flagged were corrected or left out.

source.name: Web pages cited on each question

items.question: Which is the largest ocean on Earth?
items.explain: Britannica describes the Pacific as by far the largest ocean, covering about one-third of the globe and twice the area of the Atlantic.

items.question: Which explorer gave the Pacific Ocean a name meaning "the peaceful sea"?
items.explain: Magellan named the ocean El Mar Pacifico, which means "the peaceful sea".

items.question: Which ocean trench holds the deepest known point in Earth's oceans?
items.explain: The Mariana Trench in the Pacific holds the Challenger Deep, the deepest known point on Earth, far deeper than Mount Everest is high.

items.question: What is the chemical symbol for gold?
items.explain: Gold's symbol Au comes from its Latin name, aurum, and its atomic number is 79.

items.question: What is the chemical symbol for silver?
items.explain: Silver's symbol Ag is short for its Latin name, argentum.

source.title: What Is The Chemical Symbol For Gold?

items.question: Which planet is the largest in our solar system?
items.explain: NASA calls Jupiter the largest planet in the solar system, big enough that about 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.

items.question: What is the Great Red Spot on Jupiter?
items.explain: NASA describes the Great Red Spot as a giant storm bigger than Earth.

items.question: Jupiter takes its name from the king of the gods in which ancient culture?
items.explain: NASA notes that Jupiter is named for the king of the ancient Roman gods.

items.question: Who made the first detailed observations of Jupiter in 1610, using a small homemade telescope?
items.explain: NASA says Galileo Galilei made the first detailed observations of Jupiter in 1610 with a small homemade telescope.

items.question: How many planets are in our solar system?
items.explain: NASA lists eight planets, from Mercury to Neptune, plus five officially recognized dwarf planets.

items.question: Which planet is closest to the Sun?
items.explain: NASA identifies Mercury as the closest planet to the Sun and also the smallest.

items.question: Which planet is the hottest in our solar system?
items.explain: Venus is hotter than Mercury because its thick atmosphere is full of carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas.

items.question: What is the capital city of Australia?
items.explain: Canberra is the federal capital of Australia, even though Sydney and Melbourne are larger cities.

items.question: How many bones are in a typical adult human skeleton?
items.explain: Adults have 206 bones. Children have more because some bones fuse together as they grow.

items.question: Which is the largest hot desert in the world?
items.explain: Britannica calls the Sahara of northern Africa the largest hot desert in the world.

items.question: If a desert is defined simply as a place with very little rainfall, which continent is technically the largest desert?
items.explain: Guinness notes that by the rainfall definition, Antarctica, at about 14 million square kilometres, is technically the largest desert.

items.question: Who painted the Mona Lisa?
items.explain: Leonardo da Vinci began the Mona Lisa around 1503 and it was still in his studio when he died in 1519.

items.question: In which museum does the Mona Lisa hang?
items.explain: The Mona Lisa hangs behind bulletproof glass in the Louvre in Paris and has been in the museum's collection since 1804.

items.question: Which of these mammals lays eggs?
items.explain: The platypus is a monotreme, a group of mammals that lay eggs.

items.question: What is the largest organ of the human body?
items.explain: MedlinePlus states that the skin is the largest organ of the body.

source.title: Skin layers: MedlinePlus Medical Encyclopedia Image

items.question: Which gas do plants take in from the air to carry out photosynthesis?
items.explain: In photosynthesis, green plants use light energy to turn water and carbon dioxide into oxygen and energy-rich compounds.

items.question: Which substance in plant leaves captures light energy for photosynthesis?
items.explain: Chlorophyll in the leaves absorbs light energy, which the plant uses to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.

items.question: What is the hardest naturally occurring substance on Earth?
items.explain: Diamond is the hardest naturally occurring substance and sits at 10 on the Mohs scale of mineral hardness.

source.title: Is Diamond the Hardest Substance on Earth?

items.question: Which chemical element is diamond made entirely of?
items.explain: Diamond is pure carbon, with each atom tightly bonded to four neighbours, which gives it its hardness.

source.title: Is Diamond the Hardest Substance on Earth?

items.question: How many pieces does each player start with in a standard game of chess?
items.explain: Each side starts with sixteen pieces: one king, one queen, two rooks, two bishops, two knights and eight pawns.

items.question: How many squares are on a chessboard?
items.explain: A chessboard has 64 squares of alternating colours.

source.title: How to Play Chess: Learn the Rules & 7 Steps To Get You Started - Chess.com

items.question: Which chess piece is the only one that can jump over other pieces?
items.explain: Pieces cannot move through other pieces, except that the knight can jump over them.

source.title: How to Play Chess: Learn the Rules & 7 Steps To Get You Started - Chess.com

items.question: What is the official currency of Japan?
items.explain: The yen, written ¥ or 円, is the official currency of Japan.

items.question: Who wrote the play Romeo and Juliet?
items.explain: Romeo and Juliet was written by William Shakespeare around 1594–96 and first published in 1597.

items.question: In which Italian city is Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet set?
items.explain: Shakespeare sets the play in Verona, Italy.

items.question: In Shakespeare's play, which family does Romeo belong to?
items.explain: Romeo is the son of the house of Montague, while Juliet is a Capulet.

source.title: Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare

items.question: Which mountain is the highest in the world above sea level?
items.explain: Mount Everest's summit is about 8,849 metres above sea level, higher than any other mountain on Earth.

source.title: Highest Mountain in the World - Tallest Mountain

items.question: Which animal is the largest known to have ever lived on Earth?
items.explain: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever existed, bigger than any dinosaur.

source.title: What Is the Largest Animal on Earth?

items.question: How many days does a leap year have?
items.explain: A common year has 365 days. A leap year adds February 29, making 366.

items.question: How many chambers does a healthy human heart have?
items.explain: The heart has four chambers: the left and right atria on top and the left and right ventricles below.

items.question: Which country gave the Statue of Liberty to the United States?
items.explain: The statue was a gift from the people of France, presented in 1884 to mark the alliance between the two nations.

source.title: The French Connection - Statue Of Liberty National Monument (U.S. National Park Service)

items.question: Which metal is liquid at normal room temperature?
items.explain: Mercury is the only elemental metal that is liquid at room temperature. It melts at about −38.8 °C.

items.question: Which vitamin does human skin produce when it is exposed to sunlight?
items.explain: Ultraviolet rays from sunlight striking the skin trigger the body to make vitamin D.

source.title: Vitamin D - Health Professional Fact Sheet

items.question: Who was the first person to walk on the Moon?
items.explain: Neil Armstrong, commander of Apollo 11, was the first human to set foot on the Moon in July 1969.

items.question: What was the Great Pyramid of Giza originally built to be?
answers: A temple to the sun god
items.explain: The Great Pyramid was built as a royal tomb for the Egyptian pharaoh Khufu.

items.question: What did the Titanic strike on its maiden voyage in 1912, causing it to sink?
items.explain: The Titanic hit an iceberg in the North Atlantic on the night of April 14, 1912, and sank in the early hours of April 15.

items.question: In which country is Mount Kilimanjaro, Africa's highest mountain?
items.explain: Kilimanjaro stands in Tanzania, near the Kenyan border, and rises to about 5,895 metres.

items.question: In the model most commonly taught in English-speaking countries, how many continents are there?
items.explain: The standard model counts Asia, Africa, North America, South America, Antarctica, Europe and Australia/Oceania, which makes seven.

items.question: The Eiffel Tower was built in 1889 as the centrepiece of which event in Paris?
items.explain: The tower was built for the 1889 Paris Exposition, the World's Fair, and served as its entrance gateway.

items.question: At what temperature does pure water boil at sea level?
items.explain: Under standard sea-level pressure, water boils at 100 °C (212 °F).

items.question: Which novel gave the world the idea of Big Brother and the Thought Police?
items.explain: George Orwell's 1949 novel Nineteen Eighty-Four invented concepts such as Big Brother and the Thought Police.

items.question: Which metal forms the thin outer skin of the Statue of Liberty?
items.explain: The statue is made of thin copper sheets over an inner structure of iron and steel.

items.question: Which Swedish astronomer based a temperature scale on the freezing and boiling points of water?
items.explain: In 1742 Anders Celsius created a temperature scale using the freezing and boiling points of water, and it carries his name.

items.question: Which continent is the largest by area?
items.explain: Asia covers about 44.6 million square kilometres, more than any other continent, and it is also the most populous.

source.title: The Seven Continents in Order — Size, Population & Map

items.question: Which of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World can still be seen today?
items.explain: The Great Pyramid of Giza is the last surviving member of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.

source.title: The Great Pyramid - Discover Egypt's Monuments - Ministry of Tourism and Antiquities
